messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 76
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Hotel Manager
- Trauma Type: Toxic chemical exposure
- Pcl5: 73

# Marcus

Marcus is a seventy-six-year-old man who spent the last forty-three years managing a mid-size hotel in the industrial district. He takes pride in his work—the kind of pride that comes from knowing every corner of a building, every staff member's name, every system that keeps guests comfortable. He has always been the type to arrive early and stay late, to notice what others miss.

Twenty months ago, a contractor's crew was performing routine maintenance in the basement storage area. Marcus was reviewing inventory when he smelled something acrid, chemical. He found the workers had accidentally punctured a corroded pipe containing industrial-grade cleaning solvent. The substance had pooled and begun to vaporize. Marcus, trying to be helpful, tried to contain the spill himself before calling for emergency services. He spent perhaps fifteen minutes in the space, breathing the fumes, before the fire department arrived and evacuated the building.

He was hospitalized for three days with chemical pneumonitis. The doctors said he was fortunate—his exposure could have been far worse. He recovered physically within weeks. But something else did not recover.

Marcus cannot be in the basement anymore. He has tried. He puts on a mask, descends the stairs, and within moments his chest tightens as though the air itself has become toxic. His heart races. He becomes convinced he smells the chemical again, though the space was thoroughly decontaminated months ago. He leaves quickly, sometimes stumbling in his haste to reach the ground floor. His assistant manager now handles all basement matters, but Marcus feels the weight of this delegation as a failure.

The hotel itself has become smaller. Marcus finds himself avoiding certain hallways where the basement entrance sits. He takes the longer route to his office. When guests ask about amenities in the lower level—the storage of extra linens, the backup generator room—Marcus's jaw tightens. He answers their questions but feels a strange sense of dread, as though the building itself has become unreliable, dangerous in ways he cannot control.

At night, Marcus lies awake. He replays those fifteen minutes in the basement, but his mind alters them. In these versions, he collapses. The fumes are thicker. He does not make it to the stairs. He lies on the concrete floor while the chemical burns his lungs. Sometimes he wakes gasping, certain he smells that acrid scent, though his apartment is clean and sealed. He checks the windows. He opens doors to air out rooms that need no airing.

His ex-wife calls occasionally. They divorced fifteen years ago, but she still worries about him. She has noticed he sounds tired. She asks if he is sleeping. Marcus tells her he is fine. This is not entirely untrue and not entirely false.

He has reduced his hours at the hotel, telling ownership he is thinking about retirement. The truth is more complicated. He still wants to work, still wants to feel useful, but the building where he spent four decades now holds something he cannot name—not quite fear, not quite distrust, but something in between. A sense that safety is temporary, that invisible threats exist in ordinary places, that his competence and decades of experience cannot protect him from what he cannot see.

Marcus continues to come to work. He manages from his office more than the floor. He wonders sometimes if this is what aging feels like, or if it is something else entirely.
